inline.s: The foolish fall into being and non-being, discriminating various causes and conditions.
They cannot know the manifold existences—unborn, and with no maker;
The ground of the beginningless mind: mind alone, and nothing seen.”
“Since there is no beginningless object, from what could mind arise?
If a thing arises without anything, the poor should be rich.
If mind arises without an object, I pray the Buddha will explain it to me;
If all is without a cause, then there is neither mind nor object.”
“Since mind itself is unborn, it is free from the three realms and their making;
It is by way of the jar, the cloth, and the horn that one says the rabbit’s horn is not.
Therefore one should not say that the dharmas of those marks have no cause;
Where being has no cause, it is not; and that non-being is not established as non-being.
So too with the dependent: without it, likewise; they arise in mutual dependence;
If one thing depends upon another, then some other thing arises.
Then that which is depended upon first would exist of itself without a cause;
And if that has yet another support, that support too has a support.
Thus it would be endless, and not a single dharma would exist;
As illusions appear in many forms depending on wood and leaves,
So it is with beings: by depending on things, all manner of things appear;
By the power of the magician, the foolish see illusory forms.
Yet in the wood and the leaves no illusion at all is to be found;
But if it depends upon a thing, then this dharma is destroyed.
Since what is seen is not two, how could there be any discrimination?
In discrimination there is no false imagining, and discrimination itself is not.
Because discrimination is absent, there is no birth-and-death and no nirvāṇa;
Since there is nothing discriminated, discrimination does not arise.
How is it that mind does not arise, and yet mind-only is established?
The distinctions of the mental are immeasurable, yet none of them is real;
There is no reality and no liberation, and no worlds at all;
Whatever the foolish discriminate is not to be found outside.
Habit-energy disturbs and muddies the mind, so that it appears like images;
All dharmas of being and non-being are altogether unborn.
They are only what one’s own mind displays, utterly apart from discrimination;
The teaching that all dharmas arise from conditions is for the foolish, not for the wise.
The mind’s own nature is liberated; the pure mind is where the noble ones dwell;
The Sāṃkhyas, the victorious ones, and the naked ascetics, the brahmins and the Īśvara-worshippers,
All fall into the view of non-being and stray from the meaning of stillness;
Unborn, without own-nature, stainless and empty, like an illusion.”
“The Buddhas and the present Buddha—for whom do they speak thus?
For the cultivator of the pure mind, who is free of all views and conjectures.”
“The Buddhas speak for such as these, and so do I;
If all is mind, where does the world abide?
For what reason is the great earth seen, and beings coming and going,
Like birds roaming through space, following after discrimination?
Without support and without abiding, they walk as though treading the earth;
So it is with beings: they follow false discrimination.
They course through their own mind as a bird moves through space;
The images of body, wealth, and land—the Buddha teaches that they arise from mind alone.”
“Pray tell us of the image that is mind-only: by what cause, and how, does it arise?”
“The images of body, wealth, and land all turn about through habit-energy.
They also arise from discrimination that is not in accord with principle;
The outer object is a false imagining, and the mind arises taking that object as its condition.
When one understands that the object is mind-only, discrimination does not arise;
If one sees the nature of false imagining, name and meaning do not coincide.
Apart from the perceived and the perceiving, one is freed from all that is conditioned;
When name and meaning are both abandoned—this is the Dharma of the Buddhas.
If one seeks awakening apart from this, one has no awareness of self or other;
If one can see the world as free from the perceived and the perceiving,
Then there arises no discrimination of the name and the named;
Because one sees one’s own mind, false names and words cease.
Not seeing one’s own mind, one gives rise to that discrimination;
The four aggregates have no form or mark, and their number cannot be got.
The great elements differ in nature—how do they together produce form?
Because they are free of all marks, the made and the maker are not.
If form apart from form had a mark, why would the aggregates not arise?
If one sees the markless, one abandons both aggregates and sense-fields.
Then the mind too is free, because one sees that dharmas are without self;
From the differences of faculties and objects, the eight kinds of consciousness are born.
Within that which is without marks, these three marks are all abandoned;
The mental consciousness, taking the ālaya as its object, gives rise to the grasping of self and mine.
And when one knows that the two graspings of consciousness are all abandoned,
One contemplates and sees freedom from unity and difference, and so is unmoved.
Free from self and mine, the two kinds of false discrimination
Are unborn and without increase, and are not the cause of consciousness.
Since the made and the maker are abandoned, once ceased they do not arise again;
The world has no maker, and is free from the marks of maker and made.”
“Pray explain to us false imagining and mind-only.”
“One’s own mind displays all manner of things, and one discriminates their various forms;
Not understanding what the mind displays, one falsely grasps it as outside the mind;
Through unwise awareness, one gives rise to the view of non-being.
How is it that toward existing things the mind does not become attached?
One discriminates neither being nor non-being, and so does not arise toward being.
Understanding that what is seen is mind-only, discrimination does not arise;
Because discrimination does not arise, the support is turned and one clings to nothing.
Thus one sets aside the four theses—that dharmas have a cause, and the like;
These are but different names; none of what they posit is established.
One should know that the maker-cause too is not established;
To set aside the maker, one speaks of the concurrence of causes and conditions.
To set aside the fault of permanence, one says conditions are impermanent;
The foolish say impermanent, but in truth there is no arising or ceasing.
One does not see any dharma of destruction that can do anything;
How could an impermanent dharma be able to produce anything?
Devas, humans, asuras, ghosts, beasts, and Yama’s realm, and the rest—
Beings are born among them; this I call the six paths.
By karma high, middling, and low, they receive birth among them;
Guarding all good dharmas, one attains the supreme liberation.”
“The Buddha has spoken to the monks of the births they receive;
Thought after thought, all is arising and ceasing—pray expound this for me.”
“Form after form does not pause, and mind after mind too arises and ceases;
For my disciples I teach that the thoughts they receive pass away and change.
In form after form there is discrimination, and in arising and ceasing likewise;
Discrimination is beings; apart from discrimination they are not.
For this reason I teach the arising of thought after thought;
If one is free of the grasping that holds to form, there is neither arising nor ceasing.
The conditioned and the unconditioned, ignorance and suchness, and the rest—
Because of the two dharmas there is arising; without the two, there is suchness.
If that conditioned and unconditioned, the dharmas of arising, are different,
Then permanence and the like, together with the conditions, would have maker and made.
That is what the Great Muni and all the Buddhas have taught;
But to have a maker and a made is no different from the non-Buddhists.
For my disciples I teach that the body is the suffering world;
It is also the world’s origination, and cessation and the path are all complete.
Because ordinary folk falsely discriminate and grasp the three natures,
They see a grasped and a grasping, in worldly and transcendent dharmas alike.
Because I first contemplated dependence, I spoke of grasping at own-nature;
Now, to set aside all views, one should not falsely discriminate.
To seek faults is not the Dharma, and it leaves the mind unsettled;
All this arises from the two graspings; without the two, there is suchness.
If ignorance, craving, and karma give rise to consciousness and the rest,
Then false thoughts must have a cause, and that is the fault of endlessness.
The unwise speak of all dharmas, and there are four kinds of destruction;
